en: The Collected Explanations of the Treatise Compiled by Shi Dunlun, Volume Thirty-Seven,
Chapter on Power (9b), Chapter on Power.
The preceding section clarified that reality is the very object of realization;
since there is something realized,
it cannot be merely empty.
Only when sentient beings have reached maturity does one manifest great supernormal powers to inspire faith and enable them to attain the fruits of sainthood.

If bodhisattvas seek to realize the fruit by practicing the correct path and manifesting great supernatural transformations for the sake of both self-benefit and the benefit of others, [they must first ensure the maturity of beings].
If the Munis, having distinguished their own buddha-activities, give rise to great compassion and exert themselves to deliver sentient beings by manifesting such majestic power,
it is therefore called the "Chapter on Majestic Power" (*Prabhāva-paṭala*).
It is explained after the "Chapter on Ultimate Reality" (*Tattvārtha-paṭala*).
Furthermore, Master Yuan said:
"Why is this explained next?
It is because, based on the ultimate reality, its wondrous function is sovereign."
Therefore, it is explained next.
Among the seven dharmas of the five stages, the first three have already been discussed;
next, the fourth is explained.
The *Dìchí jīng* (Kṣitigarbha-sūtra) simply refers to this as the "Chapter on Power.
In the text, there is first a question followed by an answer.
Within the answer, there are three parts.
First, two types are briefly distinguished;
next, five types are explained in detail;
finally, they are shown to be subsumed within three kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The first three are as follows:
the power of the noble ones (*ārya-prabhāva*) consists of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
The first five are shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
The sixth belongs exclusively to the noble ones (*ārya*);
being able to fully attain all six is called "noble power" (*āryaprabhāva*).
This is according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
Although a bodhisattva possesses residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), because their active afflictions (*anuśaya*) are exhausted, they are said to have "exhausted the outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*).
This constitutes the attainment of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows according to their respective degree.
Second, the power of the Dharma is explained.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there is merely a listing of names;
as for the teachings contained herein, such as the passage on the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, they appear later in the text.
Regarding the third [topic], the power of innate majesty (*sahaja-prabhāva*), Jing says:
If explained according to the Hīnayāna interpretation,
by first separately cultivating the provisions of merit,
one attains numerous qualities such as the innate wisdom of recollection (*smṛti-jñāna*).
That which arises simultaneously with the body and is capable of spontaneously recollecting and cognizing past events and so forth is called the power of co-nascence (*sahaja-bala*). This is because,
in addition to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), there exists this power of co-nascence.
In the detailed explanation of the five types below, the innate power (*sahaja-bala*) is explained as follows:
it is the capacity by nature to recollect the events of past lives (*jātaka*),
and to be able to endure all great sufferings over long periods of time for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, when he is born in the Tuṣita Heaven,
and even until the time of his Great Parinirvāṇa, the earth shakes and the stars fall;
such phenomena constitute the power of simultaneous birth.
This is not due to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Rather, it is because the eye of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), which was brought about by the Bodhisattva’s prior accumulation of provisions, is able to see afar and the ear is able to hear afar;
this is precisely what is meant by the "purification of the six sense faculties" (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Up to the point of being able to know matters such as past lives is called the power of innate capacity (*sahaja-bala*).
Ji says:
The Buddhas achieve only the wholesome states acquired through skillful means (*upāya-kṛta-kuśala*), but do not achieve those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*).
This is because wholesome states acquired by birth are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Bodhisattvas, however, possess both types.
What is now called "innate power" (*sahaja-prabhāva*) refers precisely to wholesome skillful means (*upāya-kuśala*).
Because one has practiced it in previous lives and it is now born together with the body, it is termed "innate power.
It is not what is designated as "wholesome acquired at birth" (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*).
Regarding the detailed exposition herein,
the five chapters are first opened and subsequently explained in sequence.
Within the former [section], as the old treatise states:
Regarding the five types of eightfold distinctions within the aforementioned three powers,
Kuiji says this is incorrect.
What categories are these that are called the "eightfold distinctions"?
Among these, the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) has already been explained; [next are] first, the power of the noble ones (*ārya-vaśitā*);
second, the power of the Dharma (*dharma-vaśitā*);
and third, the innate power (*sahaja-vaśitā*).
These three types, in relation to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), consist of both common and uncommon varieties;
thus they further constitute two kinds,
which, added to the previous [two], total five.
The explanation of the Chinese text is divided into four sections,
as the latter two are combined.
First, the supernatural powers and their majestic efficacy are explained.
First, the six chapters are opened;
subsequently, they are examined and explained individually.
Now, as I am about to explain the text:
First, the general meaning is distinguished by way of four gates.
The first is the discernment of the essence;
this is presented here provisionally in terms of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
Regarding those who possess the full capacity:
the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear,
when attained by ordinary beings, the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas prior to or on the stages, consist solely of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
That which is attained by all Buddhas is of the nature of these seven knowledges (*jñāna*):
namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledges of suffering, origin, the path, exhaustion, and non-arising.
Among these, because these two [knowledges] take as their objects desire-realm form and sound, they are the knowledge of phenomena.
When taking pure form and sound as objects, it is the knowledge of similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*).
If taking contaminated form and sound as objects, it is the knowledge of suffering and origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna*).
If taking uncontaminated form and sound as objects, it is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Within the body that has exhausted all afflictions, it is termed the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*);
because within this body, karma, afflictions, habitual tendencies, and so forth, never arise again, it is also termed the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*).
Excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*),

the supernormal power of the divine ear (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-abhijñā*), the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*), and the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*)— as attained by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*)— are exclusively conventional knowledge.

The supernormal power of the knowledge of the realm of psychic powers (ṛddhivisaya-jñānābhijñā) attained by a Bodhisattva of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) is of the nature of five knowledges (pañcajñāna):

namely, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), and knowledge of the origin [of suffering] (samudayajñāna).
The supernormal power of knowing the differences between minds (cetaḥparyāya-jñānābhijñā) attained at the ten stages consists of seven knowledges.
The first five [knowledges], plus the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the path,
constitute the sixfold nature of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives attained by Bodhisattvas on the ten stages.
Knowledge of past events in the two lower realms consists of the two knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Because they know what is with outflows (*sāsrava*), the subsequent two knowledges are the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) also knows the past,
taking as its object the paths previously traversed in the past.
The latter is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Therefore, the subsequent explanation of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*) states:
"Furthermore, by means of the knowledge that recollects past lives, one recollects former births."
For the sake of all sentient beings, he reveals the various types of most rare and difficult practices and ascetic austerities performed by Bodhisattvas in previous lives,
so that they may give rise to pure faith toward the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra states:
"That which you practice is the bodhisattva path.
From this, we know that the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) also takes the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) as its object.
Therefore, there is path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*).
There is also cessation-knowledge (*nirodha-jñāna*) that knows previously realized cessations.
This excludes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
If these are the eight types of knowledge possessed by the Buddhas,
they exclude conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

As for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-abhijñā*), when it is attained by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows if it takes the exhaustion of outflows as its object.
That is, it consists of six types of knowledge:

namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (kṣaya-jñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
This excludes the knowledge of the [other] three truths and the knowledge of others' minds.
That which is attained within the body of one whose outflows are exhausted is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows;
it is of the nature of the ten knowledges.
Bodhisattvas of the ten stages also attain the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows according to their respective degrees, and it is likewise of the nature of six knowledges.
The supernormal power of the destruction of outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā) attained by all Buddhas, when taking the destruction of outflows as its object, consists of five knowledges;
when it is realized within the body of one who has destroyed the outflows, it consists of nine knowledges in nature,
excluding conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Second, the explanation of how they receive their names:
the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) is named after both its objective basis and its meaning;
the supernormal power of the realization through knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) is named after both its essence and its meaning.
The supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye and ear is named according to the substance and meaning of its basis.
Now, as for the supernormal power of the divine eye also being called the supernormal power of the knowledge that sees birth and death,
it is named according to the substance and meaning of its object.
The supernormal power of realization through the knowledge of the distinctions between minds is named after its functional capacity, its object, its essence, and its meaning.
The supernormal power of realization through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is named after its object, its essence, and its meaning.
Regarding the obstacles countered by the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*):
the first five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) possess two kinds of obstacles, namely the obstacle of nature (*svabhāva-āvaraṇa*) and the obstacle of objects (*vastu-āvaraṇa*).

"Nature" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of the lower stages, such as the desire realm, which obstruct the essential nature of the five supernormal powers of the higher meditative stages from being accomplished; this is termed the "obstacle of nature."

Although one has removed the obscurations of nature and accomplished the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there still remains an obscuration of the faculties that prevents the fundamental non-cognition from being manifest in its function; this is called the "obscuration of phenomena" (*vastv-āvaraṇa*).
This obscuration of phenomena is precisely the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
The general accomplishment of this matter is achieved by removing the obstacles to the class born of maturation (*vipākaja*);
as for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), there is only the obstacle of nature (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*).
Once the obstacle of nature is removed, one immediately attains the exhaustion of outflows.
Those of the two vehicles, having fully severed the two obstacles, give rise to the supernormal powers.
Ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and bodhisattvas prior to the stages suppress the obstacle of the nature of phenomena and give rise to the five supernormal powers.

Bodhisattvas on the ten stages merely suppress the innate obstacles (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*) and sever the objective obstacles (*vyañjana-āvaraṇa*), whereby they immediately attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Since those objective obstacles are subsumed under the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), by realizing the principle of *tathatā* and severing the cognitive obstacles, they immediately attain the application of supernormal powers.
The "obstructions of nature" (prakṛti-āvaraṇa) are precisely the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward, although the coarse afflictions of the upper and middle grades are suppressed, the subtle afflictions still temporarily manifest.
It is only from the eighth stage upward that the subtle ones are suppressed, and they are suddenly severed by the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Therefore, it is known that for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the innate obstacles to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are merely suppressed and not severed.
For the Buddhas, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) function spontaneously without further removing obstacles,
because at the stage of the Vajra-mind (*vajracitta*), all obstacles to the six supernormal powers have been suddenly and completely severed.
Within the four clarifications, three degrees, and five supernormal powers,
if one considers them from the perspective of a bodhisattva,
it appears there are no other degrees.
Because one knows the minds of the formless realm through the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the form realm,
there is only the crossing of faculties and the crossing of persons,
as they are compared by way of their common characteristics.
Because people have superior or inferior capacities and their faculties are either high or low,
those of the Two Vehicles possess all three perfections,
as explained above in the thirty-third fascicle.
Regarding matters of form and sound, there should be those who transcend the faculties and those who are transcended by them.
Those with inferior faculties do not know the spheres of superior faculties;
those of inferior capacity do not know the spheres of superior capacity.
Question: In the Hīnayāna, the untainted supernormal power of knowing others' minds requires the practice of the four lower modes of the Path before one can know another's untainted mind.
What is the position regarding this meaning in the Mahāyāna school?
The Tripitaka Master says:
"Losing the four practices performed for the sake of the Path constitutes the preparatory stage (upāya);
subsequently, one gives rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava) state."
It is not necessary to perform a formal practice to know that mind.
When knowing another's mind that is with outflows (*sāsrava*), one must first perform the eight modes of contemplation regarding suffering and its origin before one can know it.
Furthermore, a mind without outflows (*anāsrava*) knows a mind with outflows.
Just as the Buddha’s supernormal power of knowing others’ minds is entirely untainted (anāsrava) and knows all tainted and untainted minds,
so it is explained in the detailed exposition.
The first explanation of the supernormal power of divine knowledge (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) is divided into three parts.
The first opens with two chapters:
first, the power of transformation (*pariṇāmika*), and second, the power of creation (*nairmāṇika*).
The second part provides a detailed explanation;
the third part generally clarifies the two types of karma.
That which undergoes transformation based on its substantial basis is termed "change."
That which suddenly appears within non-existence is termed "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).
Within our own school, it is judged that while "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) applies generally,
the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) is not itself a supernormal power (*abhijñā*), but rather the fruit of such a power.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna classification, these transformative powers are the fruits of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*) and are also subsumed under supernormal knowledge.
Furthermore, according to the Hīnayāna classification, supernormal powers are wholesome (*kuśala*).
The mind of transformation is neutral (avyākṛta).
This is not the case in the Mahāyāna;
in the Mahāyāna, the mind of transformation can be either wholesome or neutral.
If a transformation is produced for the sake of benefiting others, it is wholesome;
if it is produced merely in a general sense, it is neutral.
All transformations of the Buddhas are exclusively wholesome.
Baso said:
"This supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) is the object to be transformed.
Why, then, is it said here that the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats capable of transformation [is the subject], because it can transform and create this object?"
Therefore, the object is called "transformation" (pariṇāma) by way of its perception;
furthermore, although the transformed object is mentioned,
the intention is to clarify that it is called "transformation" because it is a supernormal power (abhijñā).
The "capable transformation" (nengbian) belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*).
By mentioning the "transformed" (*suobian*), the function of the "capable transformation" is indicated.
In the detailed explanation, the "capable transformation" is explained first, followed by the "capable emanation" (*nenghua*).
In the first transformation, there is first the question, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there is first the opening of the eighteen transformations,
followed by the detailed interpretation according to their names.
Regarding the term "grandfather," as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*,
at the beginning of the kalpa, human beings were by nature pure and upright, but later they gradually became corrupt and shallow.
Thereupon, there was one person who had previously engaged in the occupation of a thief and was first born into the realm of hungry ghosts;
because he was born first, he was called the "grandfather.
Those born after him—
From the very beginning, they are all called "grandfathers.
Regarding the transformation [of elements], it says:
"If one forms the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that upon this earth there is water, it immediately becomes water exactly as it is, and not otherwise," and so forth.
Jingyun asked:
"Its nature is originally that of earth;
how can it be transformed so as to become water?"
The answer is:
If one follows the principles of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa),
each of those stages arises from the seeds of the stage of all sentient beings.
Although they occupy the same location, they are distinct according to their respective seeds;
all are with outflows (sāsrava).
It is precisely at this location that the Buddhas perceive the stage of the ground (bhūmi).
This earth is untainted (anāsrava);
it arises from the untainted seeds of all Buddhas,
intended to provide sentient beings with the utility of water.
Thereupon, by striking the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom with the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation,
it causes the earth not to arise and causes the water-element to produce water;
this water is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Taking this as a condition, it can cause the earth-element of sentient beings to cease and the water-element to arise;
therefore, it is called "transformation.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Because the consciousness of the practitioner serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
the consciousnesses of other people transform the earth into water and so forth;
this may also be understood according to the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
All phenomena are nothing but consciousness alone.
Although they subsequently transform into various forms, these are not matter;
though appearing as matter, they are merely the measure of consciousness.
Because that which acts as the perfuming agent is mind alone and not matter, there exist only mental seeds;
furthermore, when the seeds of consciousness arise and produce consciousness, they transform into what appears as matter.
The Bodhisattva understands this principle through his revolving awareness.
Therefore, one is able to transform earth into water and so forth without any obstruction.
This is also like Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed: both are merely the measure of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra), and there is no separate, real color or fixed reality of size.
The Bodhisattva realizes this;
desiring to cause sentient beings to give rise to faith,
he manifests Mount Sumeru entering into a mustard seed.
In logic, the unreal is contained within the real. Question:
When Bodhisattvas of the same stage and equal practice both manifest supernatural powers, why is this so?
One wishes to transform earth into water;
another wishes to transform earth into fire.
Do they each succeed in their transformation?
Answer: This is explained according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
If two bodhisattvas possess equal power, the transformations they produce cannot both be established.
Among them, if one bodhisattva focuses exclusively on the perception of fire, [the other’s transformation will not be established].
If one bodhisattva does not focus his thought on water, but instead contemplates, "I shall transform earth into water to save sentient beings," then at that time,
when the two persons attempt to transform fire, the task of turning it into water will not succeed.
One should know that when the mind that performs all actions is unified in a single direction, nothing remains unaccomplished; as the sutra says:
"If the mind is restrained in one place, there is no task that cannot be achieved."
He asked again:
"Within the bodies of all Buddhas, the phenomena of birth and death, the seeds of foul colors and defilements—all these are entirely absent.
How, then, can they manifest foul colors?"
The commentary states:
Although the Buddha’s body is free from the defiled seeds of the three realms,
he manifests it because he wishes to cause sentient beings— who are attached to desire and hatred, and who perceive beauty and ugliness— to [attain liberation].
How does that which is good transform into evil?
As for its mechanism:
as one follows the mind of compassionate vows, images of both good and evil immediately appear within it.
It appears to have both the semblance and the reality of goodness;
this reality is untainted (*anāsrava*).
By taking this as a condition, it causes those sentient beings' unwholesome physical forms to cease and wholesome ones to arise.
Tài says:

Regarding the statement that one gives rise to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of beauty or ugliness toward sentient beings who are "neither" (of both), there is a certain sentient being whose form is neither beautiful nor ugly; this is called "neither."
When a bodhisattva contemplates those beautiful and ugly forms with understanding,
then the characteristics of beautiful and ugly forms manifest exactly as they are;
or it may be the reverse.
Just as other Buddhas, despite possessing supernatural powers, cannot transform the five sense objects (pañca-viṣaya) into actual sense organs capable of seeing forms and so forth;
these [objects] resemble the five sense organs but are not the actual five sense organs.
Although the elements such as earth and water are external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) whose essential natures (*svabhāva*) differ from one another,
how could water be transformed into fire?
It can only be that the substance of water ceases and a distinct substance of fire arises.
Within this, it is capable of performing the function of transformation;
by the power of the Buddha, he causes even fire to possess the quality of warmth,
and thus takes that very quality of warmth as the essence of fire.
If one were to alter their nature, transforming the insentient into the sentient,
there would be an increase or decrease in the realm of sentient beings;
therefore, it is impossible to alter one's nature.
In this context, the text states that it transforms into the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
The *Śāstra* says, "It should be known that form, fragrance, taste, and touch are likewise.
Thus, one knows that it pervades the five sense objects as its actual function.
This will be explained in detail later in the *Viniścaya* [section].
Regarding the seventh and eighth [powers], they are explained together as follows: "It can roll up all the kings of mountains, such as the Himavat, into a single atom (*paramāṇu*)."
Regarding the phrase "causing all things, such as the king of snow mountains, to be called 'contracting' and 'expanding,'" Cè (Cè) says:
"This corresponds to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* [passage] concerning placing a single mustard seed within Mount Sumeru."
Regarding the two interpretations by the masters of the Western lands,
one says that the explanation based on *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is identical to the preceding explanation of the landscape.
The second says:
According to the principle of causes and conditions,
all conditioned phenomena transcend verbal expression and are not fixed as either large or small.
They are neither identical nor different when viewed in relation to one another.
By this principle, they mutually accommodate one another without any contradiction.
Thus, the *Viniścaya* states:
Regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), there are three kinds of inseparability (*avinirbhāga*),
as explained in detail therein.
The Sarvāstivādins and others establish only the inseparability of conjunction (*saṃyoga-avinirbhāga*) and do not admit the other two.
Since that school does not admit that the four great elements interpenetrate one another,
we shall now explain all three according to the Mahāyāna. For the time being,
this will be discussed by way of their common inseparability.
For example, within the location of a single atom of the eye, there are seven atoms occupying the same place;
that is, the four great elements (mahābhūta) such as earth, which constitute the eye-faculty and the body-faculty, mutually interpenetrate and exist together in one location.
It is just as when many lamps in a single room shine upon one another without mutual interference;
therefore, by the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*), one can cause even the most minute atoms to enter Mount Himavat.
Now, regarding this treatise, its form is such that when rolled it is as large as small, and when unrolled it is as small as large.
As for what that sutra says about a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru,
it is not that the large is rolled up and the small is unrolled so that they may mutually contain one another.
The sūtras and śāstras appear to be in contradiction;
how should they be reconciled?
The explanation states that their intent is not contradictory.
This means that the small can contain the large, and the large is likewise as it was;
the large enters into the small, and the large is likewise as it was.
Therefore, in this treatise, this is termed "contracting and expanding" (vol-śu).
It is simply that a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru without relinquishing its small characteristic,
and Mount Sumeru can enter a mustard seed without destroying its large characteristic.
Therefore, that sūtra does not mention contraction or expansion;
thus there is no contradiction,
for their meaning is one and the same.
Regarding the phrase "the various images enter into the body":
it means causing each member of the great assembly to know for themselves that they have entered into their own bodies—
that is, causing others to each know for themselves that they have entered within the bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding those who proceed to the same class [of rebirth],
as for the gods of Increasing Brahma-Light (*brahmapurohita*),
Master Ji says:
Because they abide within the light of Mahābrahmā, they are called the Brahmā-prabhāsa Heaven.
What is meant by "benefit"?
Since they now abide before Mahābrahmā and provide benefit, they are called the Brahmā-prabhāsa-upakāra Heaven.
He is also called Brahmā-pūrvajita (Brahmā Pre-yi).
Cè states: "According to the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras..."
